subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I share a flat with Lokesh, so I saw this play out. Two weeks ago at the college canteen a senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer while about ten people laughed or looked away. Lokesh was there and said nothing; I know because Lokesh told me that night, sitting on the balcony staring at the street. Lokesh was quiet for days. Then on Friday Lokesh went and found Pooja and said, "I saw what happened and I did nothing. I am sorry." Pooja shrugged, said thanks, and then told Lokesh what it had felt like. I stood at the door. I think it cost Lokesh a lot to say it. Lokesh has already decided that next time it will be sitting beside Pooja straight away.

qa.q: What did the senior do at the college canteen?
qa.a: A senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer at the college canteen while about ten people laughed or looked away.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling during the days after the canteen?
qa.a: Lokesh felt regret and shame, staring at the street and staying quiet for days, which turned into a wish to apologise.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with the shame instead of hiding it?
qa.a: Lokesh went to Pooja, admitted watching and doing nothing, apologised, and decided to sit beside Pooja next time.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pooja to hear Lokesh's apology and then describe how it had felt?
qa.a: Pooja probably felt some relief at being seen and believed; shrugging and saying thanks before opening up suggests careful trust.

grounding: A young adult regrets watching and doing nothing, uses the shame to decide how to act next time and apologises to the person affected.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Monday. In the hostel lounge four people laughed as someone filmed Tushar tripping and spilling his tea, and no one helped. Ayesha stood at the doorway with her books, telling herself it was just a joke. Tushar left without a word. Tuesday. Ayesha could not concentrate. The picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying, and shame settled in her chest. Thursday. Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door. "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry. If it happens again I will come over to you at once." Tushar looked surprised, then said, "Thanks for saying so." They sat and drank tea.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say when knocking on Tushar's door?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry."

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: Ayesha felt shame and guilt, unable to concentrate as the picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying.

qa.q: What turning point on Thursday moved Ayesha from shame to action?
qa.a: Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door, apologised for watching and promised to come over at once next time.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when Ayesha knocked and apologised?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt surprised and a little comforted to learn that one person had noticed and cared; the thanks and the shared tea suggest relief.

grounding: A young adult regrets having watched and done nothing, and apologises to the person affected while deciding how to act next time.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
In the student bar in Dublin, three lads from Bilal's course started joking about Rania's headscarf, loud enough for her table to hear. “Is it hiding a bad hair day?” one said. Others laughed.
Bilal sat right there. He stared at his drink. He told himself it wasn't his fight.
Rania gathered her things and left without a word.
Bilal didn't sleep well. By morning the feeling was clear: it was shame, and hiding from it would make it worse.
He found Rania outside the library. “I was there last night. I should have said something. I'm sorry.” She looked at him for a long moment. “Thanks for saying it.”
He wrote one line in his notes app: Next time, say “Not funny, lads,” and sit with her.

qa.q: Where did the joking happen?
qa.a: It happened in the student bar in Dublin.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling the next morning?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and regretful, and knew that hiding from the feeling would make it worse.

qa.q: Is Bilal's plan for next time a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; a short line like "Not funny, lads" and sitting with Rania is simple and safe, so he's more likely to actually do it.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt when Bilal apologised?
qa.a: She seemed cautious but touched; after being mocked while people watched, an honest apology may have eased some of the hurt.

grounding: Shows a young man who watched a classmate being mocked and did nothing, then uses his shame to apologise and plan how to act next time.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
At the hostel mess on Saturday night, three seniors made Naveen stand on a bench and sing while they threw bread at him. Forty students watched. Nazia was one of them. She kept eating, eyes down.
All night she saw his face.
On Sunday morning she knocked on the first-years' room. “Naveen, I was in the mess. I didn't do anything. I'm really sorry.”
He shrugged, but his eyes were red.
“Will you come with me to the warden? I'll tell her what I saw.”
They went together. The warden listened to both, thanked Nazia, called the anti-ragging cell that morning and moved the three seniors to another floor while it was looked into.
Nazia told herself: never again with my eyes down.

qa.q: How many students watched in the mess?
qa.a: Forty students watched.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel through the night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed, unable to stop seeing Naveen's face.

qa.q: What did Nazia do with her guilt, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She apologised to Naveen and went with him to the warden as a witness, turning regret into action that got the seniors dealt with.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Nazia apologised?
qa.a: He seemed hurt and wary, his eyes red, but may have felt less alone knowing someone would stand with him.

grounding: Shows a young woman who watched a junior being humiliated and did nothing, then apologises and acts as a witness next morning.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Dear Irfan,
I'm writing because I couldn't say this properly in the corridor.
At the fest, when you went blank on stage and some of our own team started laughing and filming, I was in the second row. I didn't stop them. I didn't even stop smiling, because everyone else was. I've felt sick about it for three days.
I'm sorry. You didn't deserve that, and you didn't deserve silence from someone you thought was a friend.
I've already asked Kabir and Neel to delete their videos, and they did. And I've promised myself that next time someone is mocked, I'll stand up, even if I'm the only one.
If you'd like chai this week, I'm buying.
Ritu

qa.q: Where was Ritu sitting at the fest?
qa.a: Ritu was in the second row.

qa.q: How has Ritu felt since the fest?
qa.a: Ritu has felt guilty and ashamed, sick about it for three days for smiling along instead of stopping the laughter.

qa.q: What makes this letter more than just an apology?
qa.a: Ritu has already acted, getting the videos deleted, and made a clear promise about next time, which shows real change.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Irfan might feel hurt remembering the stage, but relieved and respected that Ritu owned up and acted.

grounding: A young adult writes to a friend after watching the friend mocked and staying silent, using the shame to apologise and decide how to act next time.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
You want to know why I'm running the anti-bullying stall at the fest? Okay.
I'm Seema, second year. Last semester in the canteen, a group from our class poured water over Tanvir's notes and called him "topper-bhai" while half the room filmed it. I was at the next table. I laughed once, nervously, and then just stared at my plate.
That night I couldn't sleep. I kept seeing his face, trying to smile. For a week I avoided him in the corridors, because I couldn't look at him.
Then it hit me: hiding was just doing nothing a second time. So I went up to him in the library and said, "I watched and did nothing. I'm sorry." He was quiet, then said, "Thanks for saying it. Most people pretend they weren't there."
So I've decided. Next time, I'm the one who says stop, or goes to a teacher. That's why I'm at this stall.

qa.q: What did the group pour over Tanvir's notes?
qa.a: They poured water over Tanvir's notes.

qa.q: How did Seema feel in the week after the canteen incident?
qa.a: Seema felt ashamed and guilty, lying awake and avoiding Tanvir in the corridors.

qa.q: What did Seema decide to do next time, and why is that a good use of guilt?
qa.a: To say stop or go to a teacher; it turns regret into a plan instead of more hiding.

qa.q: What might Seema's apology have meant to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir seemed quietly relieved; since most people pretended they weren't there, being acknowledged made him feel less alone 🤍

grounding: Shows a young adult who regrets watching and doing nothing, then uses that shame to apologise and decide how to act next time.
